explain: _dormīvī_ is the perfect of _dormiō_: 'I slept'. The I-form of the perfect always ends in -ī. _bene_ = 'well'.
distractors: _dormiō_ is the present: 'Today I sleep well'. For something finished you need _dormīvī_.
_dormīvistī_ is the 'you' form: 'Today you slept well'.

explain: _herī_ = yesterday. The perfect of _edō_ is _ēdī_ (the stem changes: ed- → ēd-). The thing eaten is in the accusative: _pānem_ (from _pānis_).
distractors: _edō_ is the present: 'Yesterday I eat bread'. Past needs _ēdī_.
The thing eaten needs the accusative _pānem_, not the nominative _pānis_.

explain: _bibō_ (I drink) has the perfect _bibī_ (I drank): only the ending changes. _vīnum_ = wine.
distractors: _bibō_ is the present: 'Yesterday I drink wine'.
_bibistī_ is the 'you' form: 'Yesterday you drank wine'.

explain: _surgō_ has an irregular perfect: _surrēxī_. Perfect stems have to be learned with the verb, which is why they are worth drilling in whole sentences.
distractors: _surgō_ is the present: 'This morning I get up'.
_surrēxit_ is the 'he/she' form: 'This morning he got up'.

en: Yesterday I walked to the forum.
explain: _ad_ ('to, toward') takes the accusative: _ad forum_. Verbs in -āre make their perfect with -āvī: _ambulāvī_ = I walked.
distractors: _ad_ needs the accusative _forum_; _forō_ is the ablative.
_ambulō_ is the present: 'Yesterday I walk to the forum'.
_ambulāvit_ is the 'he/she' form: 'Yesterday he walked to the forum'.

explain: _videō_ (I see) → _vīdī_ (I saw). The friend is the object, so _amīcum_ is accusative, and _meum_ ('my') copies its case, number and gender.
distractors: The friend is what I saw, so he needs the accusative _amīcum meum_, not the nominative.
_videō_ is the present: 'I see my friend'.
_meam_ is feminine, but _amīcum_ is masculine. It should be _meum_.

explain: _legō_ → _lēgī_: the vowel gets longer in the perfect. _librum_ is the accusative of _liber_ (book).
distractors: _legō_ is the present: 'Yesterday I read a book' needs the perfect _lēgī_.
The thing read is the object, so it needs the accusative _librum_.
_lēgistī_ is the 'you' form: 'Yesterday you read a book'.

en: In the evening I had dinner.
explain: _vesperī_ = 'in the evening'. _cēnāre_ is 'to dine': the Romans' main meal, _cēna_, was eaten in the afternoon or evening.
distractors: _cēnō_ is the present: 'In the evening I have dinner'.
_cēnāvistī_ is the 'you' form: 'In the evening you had dinner'.
_māne_ = in the morning: 'In the morning I had dinner'.

explain: _domī_ means 'at home' (where you are); _domum_ means 'to home' (where you are going). _labōrāvī_ = I worked.
distractors: _labōrō_ is the present: 'Yesterday I work at home'.
_labōrāvistī_ is the 'you' form: 'Yesterday you worked at home'.

en: First I washed, then I ate.
explain: Both actions are finished, so both verbs are perfect: _lāvī_ (from _lavō_) and _ēdī_ (from _edō_). _prīmum … deinde_ keeps the order.
distractors: The order is reversed: 'First I ate, then I washed'.
Both verbs are present here: 'First I wash, then I eat'.
The second verb is present (_edō_). Past needs _ēdī_.

explain: _veniō_ (I come) → _vēnī_ (I came). _domum_ ('home' as a destination) needs no preposition. Note that _veniō_ and _vēnī_ differ only in the long vowel and ending.
distractors: _domī_ = at home. For 'came home' (toward) you need _domum_.
